newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Mercenaries push PNG army chief over the edge.
newsitem.headline: Mercenaries push PNG army chief over the edge.

text.p: Underpaid and ill-equipped, the soldiers of the Papua New Guinea Defence Force have grown used to frustration in their nine-year conflict with the ragtag rebels of Bougainville island.
But when Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan secretly recruited a group of expensive foreign mercenaries to end the uprising, it was one slap in the face too many, experts say.
Defence Force Commander Brigadier General Jerry Singirok announced on Monday that he had ordered the detention of 40 African mercenaries and given Chan a 48-hour deadline to quit.

"As a professional military officer I have kept quiet and followed orders from this government as I would for any serving government of the day without questioning their orders and directives," Singirok said in an "Address to the Nation"
"I cannot remain silent for long...," he added.
In one sense, Singirok and his army should have welcomed Chan's "radical initiative" to end the conflict on Bougainville island, which lies 800 km (500 miles) northeast of the capital Port Moresby.

Under the plan as outlined to the media by Chan, the defence force would gain both training and sophisticated equipment from the mercenaries of South African-based Executive Outcomes, hired for PNG by the British company Sandline International.

PNG officials said the contract with Sandline was worth around A$36 million (US28.6 million), most of which would be spent on military hardware such as helicopter gunships to track down the Bougainville guerrillas.
Another part of the plan was the government should buy Bougainville's Panguna copper mine, a massive mine which sparked the uprising, from its Anglo-Australian owners RTZ-CRA.

But Singirok complained on Monday that the plan made neither military nor political sense. The army chief said Chan should be trying to resolve the conflict through negotiation not force and -- amid allegations of corruption -- was paying far too much for obsolete Soviet military technology no one else wanted.

Ron May, a PNG specialist at the Australian National University in Canberra, told Reuters that Singirok was appointed commander by Chan after successes in Bougainville, where he managed to rein in the violent excesses of PNG troops.
Singirok was seen as a "soldier's soldier" and was said in recent weeks to have been pushing opponents within the higher echelons of the PNG defence into retirement.

But his relations with Chan had suffered since the failure of a high-profile offensive on Bougainville last year and the troops on the island remained ill-equipped, unpopular among locals on the island and rarely received special allowances due them for their combat role.
And when Chan decided to hire the mercenaries, it appeared that he consulted little with Singirok.
"Many of them would feel resentment that Sandline had been able to get this money when they couldn't even get their allowances," said May.
"I guess a large part of it is that he was not adequately consulted about bringing the mercenaries in, it was certainly a slap in the face."

James Griffin, emeritus professor of history at the University of Papua New Guinea, said he was not surprised by Singirok's move because the hiring of Sandline had put the army in a very difficult position.
"The army has a very good cause against using mercenaries," Griffin told Australian radio.

"Here you have got this very large sum of money being spent on them when the army has been languishing over in Bougainville, not even, with sufficient food...and here Sir Julius can find the money to bring in these mercenaries who have no (local) experience whatsoever."
